paper.title: Enhancing diagnosis of Parkinson's Disease through a deep learning-based multiclass interpretation of DaTscan SPECT images.
paper.abstract:
Background: Early and accurate diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) remains challenging due to clinical overlap with other parkinsonian syndromes. DaTscan single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) is widely used during diagnosis; however, a subset of clinically diagnosed patients presents scans without evidence of dopaminergic deficit (SWEDD), creating diagnostic ambiguity. This study developed and validated a deep learning (DL)-based multiclass framework to distinguish PD, SWEDD, and normal controls using DaTscan SPECT images.
Methods: DaTscan images from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) were used for model development, with external validation performed using an independent cohort from Chiayi Christian Hospital. AlexNet, EfficientNet-B0, and Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures were trained and evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The best-performing model was integrated into an automated diagnostic tool, the Parkinson's Disease Detector App.
Results: EfficientNet-B0 achieved the highest accuracy for three-class classification on the PPMI dataset (94.2%), outperforming ViT (92.0%) and AlexNet (89.5%). External validation demonstrated strong generalizability (accuracy 92.4%, F1-score 95.8%). The diagnostic app achieved 90.6% accuracy in distinguishing PD and SWEDD from controls.
Conclusion: The proposed DL framework enables accurate multiclass classification of DaTscan SPECT images and shows promise as an objective adjunct for PD diagnosis. Multicenter validation is warranted.

paper.title: External validation of a machine learning model for classifying hospitalization outcomes in Asian elephants across three elephant hospitals in Thailand.
paper.abstract: Classification of hospitalization outcomes in wildlife hospitals may support clinical assessment and resource planning, but model performance can vary across institutions with different case profiles and care practices. This study evaluated a previously developed random forest model for classifying hospitalization outcomes in Asian elephants using temporally distinct 2025 data from three elephant hospitals in Thailand. The validation comprised temporal validation at the original development center and institutional validation at two additional hospitals. Because length of stay was included as a predictor, the model was evaluated as a hospitalization-course classification model rather than as an admission-time prognostic tool. The final validation cohort comprised 237 hospitalization episodes contributed by 215 elephants, including 17 deceased, 36 ongoing, and 184 recovered episodes. Overall accuracy was 0.793, compared with 0.776 for a recovered-only majority-class classifier. Macro-averaged balanced accuracy was 0.732, the prevalence-weighted one-vs-rest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was 0.854, and multiclass log loss was 0.617. Classification performance was stronger for ongoing and recovered episodes than for deceased episodes. The limited number of deceased episodes resulted in substantial uncertainty around mortality-focused performance and calibration estimates. Calibration patterns differed across outcome classes, with an overall multiclass Brier score of 0.323. In the binary deceased-versus-recovered sensitivity analysis, the AUC was 0.726 (95% confidence interval, 0.585-0.839), indicating moderate but imprecise discrimination. Overall, the model retained discriminatory information across the validation cohort, but its modest improvement over the majority-class benchmark, weaker deceased-class performance, and reliance on hospitalization-duration information warrant cautious interpretation. Further prospective evaluation is needed before routine clinical application.

paper.title: Development and validation of an explainable artificial intelligence model to predict in-hospital adverse events for patients with acute myocardial infarction.
paper.abstract: In-hospital adverse events after acute myocardial infarction (AMI) can occur abruptly and adversely affect short-term prognosis. We developed and externally validated explainable machine learning models to predict a composite of in-hospital atrial fibrillation (AF), ventricular fibrillation (VF), cardiac arrest (CA), or death using routinely available admission data. We retrospectively analyzed 7,496 patients from the MIMIC-IV database as the development cohort and 2,776 patients from Xuanwu Hospital as the external validation cohort. Predictors included demographics, medical history, and admission laboratory tests. Logistic regression, random forest, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), multilayer perceptron, and TabNet models were evaluated using five-fold cross-validation. Performance was assessed using discrimination, classification, calibration, and decision curve analysis. Latent class analysis identified three outcome clusters with distinct event-probability profiles. XGBoost achieved the best performance for the composite outcome in the development cohort (AUROC, 0.798). Predictive performance was moderate to good for AF and in-hospital death, with AUROCs of up to 0.834 and 0.870 in the development cohort and 0.803 and 0.849 in the external validation cohort, respectively. Discrimination was lower for VF and CA. SHapley Additive exPlanations highlighted neutrophil and leukocyte counts, N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide, renal function, glucose, glycated hemoglobin A1c, and prior AF as important predictors. These explainable models may support early risk stratification and help guide monitoring intensity and timely intervention in patients with AMI.

paper.title: Assessment of Coronary Inflammatory Risk From Noncontrast Cardiac Computed Tomography.
paper.abstract:
Importance: Individuals with low or minimal coronary artery calcification (CAC) are considered at low cardiovascular risk, but a substantial absolute number of cardiovascular events occur in this population; assessment of coronary inflammation using the fat attenuation index (FAI) score may identify residual inflammatory risk beyond CAC score.
Objective: To assess whether coronary inflammation measured on coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) or noncontrast cardiac CT (NCCT) identifies individuals at high cardiovascular risk independent of CAC burden.
Design, Setting, And Participants: In this cohort study, a novel artificial intelligence algorithm for measuring FAI score on NCCT was trained and tested in an independent, multicenter, longitudinal cohort of consecutive individuals undergoing clinically indicated CCTA and NCCT for CAC score between 2010 and 2021, with median (IQR) follow-up of 6.7 (4.6-10.0) years. Data were analyzed from January 2010 to March 2024.
Exposure: Agatston CAC score and coronary inflammation from both CCTA (CCTA FAI score, established biomarker) and NCCT (NC FAI score, novel biomarker).
Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary outcome was cardiovascular (CV) mortality; the secondary outcome was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), comprising myocardial infarction, new-onset heart failure, or CV death.
Results: The derivation cohort included 6818 individuals (median [IQR] age, 61 [51-71] years; 3543 female participants [52.0%]), and the external validation clinical outcomes cohort included 19 110 individuals (median [IQR] age, 56.0 [48.0-64.0] years; 9289 female participants [48.6%]). During follow-up, 536 CV deaths and 1727 MACE occurred. FAI scores independently stratified CV mortality risk across CAC score categories, with the strongest associations among individuals with CAC score of 0. Adding CCTA FAI score or NC FAI score to CAC score significantly improved risk discrimination (area under the curve increased from 0.76 to 0.81 and 0.80, respectively; P < .001), reclassification (net reclassification index), and net benefit across all risk thresholds. Among 89 CV deaths in individuals with CAC score of 0 and 138 CV deaths with CAC score of 1 through 99, 44.9% and 44.2% had NC FAI score above the 75th percentile, respectively. Among individuals with CAC score of 0, CV mortality rates increased from 1.4 to 4.0 per 1000 person-years for those with NC FAI score above the 75th percentile, and MACE rates increased from 5.9 to 13.3 per 1000 person-years.
Conclusions And Relevance: Per the results of this cohort study, NC FAI score provides prognostic performance comparable to CCTA FAI score and improves cardiovascular risk prediction and reclassification beyond CAC score. Elevated FAI score, derived from either CCTA or NCCT, should be interpreted as a risk-enhancing factor that may prompt intensification of established, evidence-based preventive measures and may serve as a potential future gatekeeper for the use of targeted anti-inflammatory treatments.

paper.title: Evaluation of a Rapid and Practical Deep Learning Framework for T1-weighted MRI-based Brain Age Estimation.
paper.abstract: Purpose To develop and evaluate a rapid brain-age estimation framework using freely available Python tools and assess the clinical relevance of brain-age gap (BAG). Materials and Methods In this retrospective study conducted from March 2025 to August 2026, T1-weighted MR images from cohorts of cognitively normal adults (n = 4,346) were divided into training, validation, and internal test sets; two cohorts (n = 315 and 209) served as external test sets. Clinical evaluation used the BICWALZS cohort (n = 954; cognitively normal and various dementias). Preprocessing used freely available Python tools only. The model was trained to predict chronological age as the reference standard. Associations of the residualized BAG with diagnosis, amyloid PET positivity, white matter hyperintensity (WMH) severity, stroke history, and longitudinal clinical worsening were evaluated using ANCOVA, logistic regression, and Cox models. Results The development cohort included 4,346 cognitively normal adults (mean age, 47.0 ± 21.2 years; 2,414 women). Chronological age prediction yielded R2 = 0.95 and MAE, 3.76 years in the internal test set and R2 = 0.69-0.90 and MAE, 4.82-5.15 years in external test sets. The residualized BAG increased across diagnostic groups (P < .001) and was associated with WMH severity (odds ratio [OR], 1.64; P < .001) and stroke history (OR, 1.46; P < .001), but not with amyloid positivity after full adjustment (P = .17), and predicted longitudinal clinical worsening (HR, 1.92). Conclusion The framework accurately predicted age, while residualized BAG was associated with diagnosis, cerebrovascular burden, and longitudinal clinical worsening. © RSNA, 2026.

paper.title: Development and external validation of machine learning models for predicting glucose trajectories after continuous intravenous insulin therapy in hyperglycemic crises.
paper.abstract:
Background And Aims: Predicting short-term blood glucose changes after initiation of continuous intravenous insulin infusion (CII) in hyperglycemic crises remains challenging because glucose trajectories are influenced by both patient-specific metabolic severity and dynamically adjusted treatment. This study aimed to develop and externally validate machine learning models for estimating retest glucose levels and glucose-lowering responses after CII initiation.
Methods: We analyzed 574 post-CII blood glucose measurements from 191 patients with hyperglycemic crises across five Japanese institutions. An independent external validation cohort included 29 patients from another institution. Two complementary models were developed using gradient-boosted decision tree algorithms: a direct retest glucose prediction model and a ΔGlu treatment-response model. We evaluated model performance using internal validation, patient-level fivefold cross-validation, and external validation. ΔGlu was defined as the decrease in blood glucose between two consecutive reassessment points.
Results: The eight-feature direct retest glucose model showed stable predictive performance in internal validation (R2 = 0.853, MAE = 76.9 mg/dL, RMSE = 106.0 mg/dL), patient-level fivefold cross-validation (R2 = 0.803 ± 0.080), and external validation (R2 = 0.802, MAE = 78.0 mg/dL, RMSE = 101.0 mg/dL). Although the eight-feature ΔGlu treatment-response model showed moderate internal performance, its external generalizability for ΔGlu prediction was limited.
Conclusions: The direct retest glucose model showed stable performance across internal and external validation, whereas ΔGlu itself was more difficult to generalize across institutions. These complementary models may support objective monitoring of short-term glucose trajectories during CII for hyperglycemic crises, although further prospective validation is warranted.

paper.title: Behavioral and psychosocial indicators for depression and anxiety risk stratification among college students: development and external validation of a machine-learning-assisted framework.
paper.abstract:
Background: Depression and anxiety symptoms are common among college students. Behavioral and psychosocial indicators may support preventive campus mental health work, but risk-stratification frameworks require external validation.
Methods: We developed a construct-level model-explanation framework using questionnaire data from a development sample. The cleaned dataset included 1,267 students; internal-validation analyses included 1,096 students for depression risk and 1,095 for anxiety risk. Risk was defined as a Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) or Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) score of 10 or higher. The primary Feature set C random-forest (RF) pipelines integrated demographic, traditional, and emerging behavioral and psychosocial indicators. Fold-specific preprocessing and percentile cutoffs were used for internal validation. Locked pipelines were applied without retraining, predictor reselection, optimization, recalibration, or threshold adjustment to an independent university sample of 1,468 students.
Results: External area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC), and Brier scores were 0.813 (95% CI, 0.776-0.848), 0.402 (0.325-0.491), and 0.090 (0.083-0.098), respectively, for depression and 0.809 (0.765-0.851), 0.205 (0.144-0.300), and 0.063 (0.056-0.070), respectively, for anxiety. Ordinary participant-level bootstrap was the primary approach, with stratified bootstrap as a sensitivity analysis. Depression calibration was close to the prevalence baseline (Brier 0.091; intercept -0.668; slope 1.401), whereas anxiety showed miscalibration (Brier 0.063 vs. baseline 0.051; intercept -1.227; slope 1.102). The models supported external discrimination and risk ranking but did not validate individual absolute-risk probabilities or clinical thresholds.
Conclusion: Behavioral and psychosocial indicators supported externally validated risk stratification in an independent university sample. Anxiety-risk findings should be interpreted as preliminary because the number of positive cases was limited. Further evaluation is needed before wider implementation.

paper.title: An explainable multimodal model integrating post-ESD mucosal defect images and clinical features to predict delayed bleeding after colorectal endoscopic submucosal dissection.
paper.abstract:
Background: Existing tools for predicting delayed bleeding (DB) after colorectal endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) use only structured clinical variables, leaving information in post-ESD mucosal defect images unused. We developed and externally validated an explainable multimodal model integrating these images with clinical features.
Methods: We retrospectively included 3,416 patients who underwent colorectal ESD at two hospitals from January 2022 through June 2026 (development cohort, n = 2,778; external validation cohort, n = 638). DB was active bleeding 6 h to 28 days after ESD, confirmed by repeat endoscopy and requiring endoscopic hemostasis. YOLOv11m-seg segmented mucosal defects, ResNet50 generated an image-derived prediction score (E-Score), and the E-Score was fused with clinical features. After LASSO feature selection, five algorithms with and without SMOTE were evaluated by fivefold stratified cross-validation. SHAP and Grad-CAM provided post-hoc feature- and image-level explanations.
Results: DB occurred in 224 patients (8.06%) in the development cohort and 53 (8.31%) in the external validation cohort (P = 0.839). The segmentation model achieved mAP50 and mAP50-95 values of 0.984 and 0.838. Six features were retained. XGBoost without SMOTE (PrismDB) performed best (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC], 0.804; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.769-0.837), with 64.73% sensitivity, 85.40% specificity, and 96.50% negative predictive value. In external validation, the AUC was 0.788 (95% CI, 0.724-0.850), sensitivity was 79.25%, specificity was 83.25%, and negative predictive value was 97.79%. Probability calibration in the development cohort under the natural event distribution showed a calibration slope of 1.101 and an intercept of + 0.227 (Brier score, 0.0584). E-Score had the highest mean absolute SHAP contribution, and representative activation maps overlapped with exposed vessels, adherent clots, and eschar.
Conclusions: PrismDB showed stable discrimination for DB after colorectal ESD. Low-risk classification did not exclude DB. Probability calibration was acceptable in the development cohort but has not been evaluated externally, and the safety of model-guided changes to postoperative care remains to be established; the companion web application demonstrates the prediction workflow.

paper.title: Two-Phase Multimodal Integration of Clinical Text and Imaging for Population-scale Screening of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events.
paper.abstract: Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) remain the leading cause of mortality worldwide. Early identification of at-risk patients is essential for timely management; however, cardiac risk estimation tools, e.g. PCE and PREVENT, often demonstrate unequal performance across demographic subgroups. Furthermore, confirmatory cardiac imaging modalities (CT, MRI) are costly, invasive, and limited to symptomatic patients. Most predictive studies define outcomes via structured billing codes, which have high error rates and institution-specific variability. We propose a multimodal AI framework enabling large-scale MACE screening using low-cost chest X-rays and clinical text. The approach consists of two phases: (i) an NLP-based pipeline to extract MACE-related outcomes from temporal clinical notes, and (ii) an imaging model trained on these weak labels to estimate MACE risk from chest X-rays, learning latent cardiopulmonary phenotypes denoting cardiovascular risk. We trained these models by automatically curating data from 36,622 patients in the MIMIC-IV-Note and MIMIC-IV-CXR datasets and validating against 250 chart-reviewed patients and 2,152 ED patients from another tertiary care center. Weak MACE labels generated by Mistral-Instruct enabled the imaging model to achieve high performance on internal (AUC = 0.81 [0.78-0.84]) and external (AUC = 0.77 [0.75-0.79]) cohorts, surpassing a fully-supervised baseline. Our findings demonstrate that weakly-supervised learning using large-scale, noisy labels derived from clinical notes substantially improves model generalizability compared with limited manually-annotated datasets. The proposed framework enables population-scale opportunistic cardiovascular screening without requiring dedicated cardiac imaging or extensive manual labeling, discovering subclinical cardiovascular risk signatures embedded within routinely collected clinical data.
